office.title: Indiana School Board Member
office.summary: A school board is the elected or appointed governing body of a public school corporation, the legal unit that runs a local school district [1, 2]. The board hires and evaluates the superintendent, adopts policies, and approves the annual budget, while the superintendent and staff run schools day to day [3]. Most boards have five or seven members serving staggered four-year terms [3]. Starting in 2026, candidates may list a political party, run as independents, or list no affiliation on the ballot, and there is no primary for these seats [2, 4].

facts.label: Term
facts.value: 4 years, with elections staggered so part of the board is chosen every two years [3]

facts.label: Elected
facts.value: At the November general election (November 3, 2026, or November 2028 for some seats); depending on the local organization plan, members represent the whole school corporation (at large) or a district within it, and some boards are wholly or partly appointed [2]

facts.label: Ballot label
facts.value: Each candidate chooses a party label, 'Independent', or no affiliation, shown next to the name; no primary and no straight-ticket voting for these races [2, 4]

facts.label: Pay
facts.value: Set by board resolution: an annual amount of no more than 10% of the lowest starting teacher salary in the school corporation, plus a capped per diem [5]

duties: Hires, evaluates and can dismiss the superintendent, and approves the hiring and firing of principals, teachers and other staff recommended by the superintendent [1, 7, 3].
Adopts the annual budget, appropriates funds and oversees school finances [1, 3].

Decides whether to ask voters to approve an operating referendum (an extra property tax levy); the board adopts the resolution and the Department of Local Government Finance reviews the ballot language for compliance with state law [8].
Approves contracts, buys and sells property, and decides on construction, repair and demolition of school buildings [1].

Bargains with the teachers' union over salary, wages and wage-related benefits such as health insurance and retirement; state law excludes teacher evaluation procedures from those bargaining subjects [9].
Writes and updates policies and rules for schools, often in a policy handbook, including the student handbook [1, 3].
Buys curricular materials, provides them to students without charge, and runs programs such as student transportation and school lunch [1].

Must adopt a process for parents and residents to ask that library material be removed as obscene or harmful to minors, review requests at public meetings and keep a public catalog of library materials [10].
Hears written appeals of student expulsions, unless the board has voted not to hear them [11].
Must take official action openly; Indiana's Open Door Law says public agencies' official action is to be conducted openly so the people may be fully informed [12, 13].

A school board member must have lived in the school corporation (and, for a district seat, the district) for at least one year before the election, and a teacher or other employee of the school corporation may not serve on its board [2].

What the board does not control: the State Board of Education adopts statewide academic standards [14], the General Assembly sets the state school funding formula in the state budget [15], and voucher (Choice Scholarship) eligibility is set by state law [16].
recent_changes: 2025: Senate Enrolled Act 287 allowed school board candidates to declare a party affiliation; the Indiana School Boards Association opposed the change, and a supporter quoted by WNDU, a Noblesville school board member, said it adds transparency [17].

2026: Candidates choose a party, 'Independent' or no affiliation on their nominating petition, and that choice appears on the ballot; a candidate claiming the Democratic or Republican party must have voted in that party's primary in the two most recent primaries they voted in, or have certification from the county party chair, or can be challenged and removed from the ballot [2].

July 2026: Chalkbeat reported, citing Indiana School Boards Association data, that 524 of 1,044 candidates chose a party, about 72% of them Republicans [18]; the Indiana Election Division's 2026 guidance and the wording of the law differ on the primary-voting test, a question county election boards decide [19].

February 2026: Senate Enrolled Act 25 set the order of school board candidates on the ballot, grouped by party, with candidates who list no affiliation placed after the party and independent candidates [20].

2025: Senate Enrolled Act 1, a property tax law, limits how much operating revenue districts can raise through taxes and restricts school referendums to statewide general elections in even-numbered years [21, 22].
2025: The same law requires districts to share operating revenue with brick-and-mortar charter schools that enroll their students, statewide starting in 2028 [21, 22].
2025: The state budget opened Choice Scholarship vouchers to all Indiana families starting in June 2026 [16].
2026: The Indianapolis Public Education Corporation, rather than the Indianapolis Public Schools board, now certifies Indianapolis Public Schools referendum questions for the ballot [20].

2023: Senate Enrolled Act 391 changed the so-called $1 law so the Indiana Department of Education can order districts that lost at least 10% of enrollment over five years to close schools under 60% capacity and offer them to charter schools [23].
2023: House Enrolled Act 1447 required school districts to set up procedures for complaints that library material is obscene or harmful to minors [10].

race_context: The district: White River Valley School District (WRV) serves western Greene County. Its high school is in Switz City, its middle school in Lyons and its elementary school in Worthington [24, 25]. Public School Review lists about 704 students in three schools; the year behind that figure is unclear [26]. Federal data show 209 students at the high school in 2023-24 [24]. Jason Walton is superintendent: the board named him interim superintendent in October 2025 and approved his contract as superintendent on March 16, 2026 [27, 28].

Board: the board has seven members, elected from township-based districts plus at-large seats [29, 30]. As of mid-2026 the members were Brock Hostetter (president, at large), Joe Decker (vice president, Jefferson II), Cleta Shake (secretary, Stafford Township), Brenden Dyer (Fairplay and Cass), Andy Davis, Miranda Hostetter and Roger Weaver [31, 32, 33]. Davis (District 5), Miranda Hostetter (District 1) and Weaver (District 3) were elected in 2024 [30].

Seats on the 2026 ballot: District 2 (Stafford), District 4 (Fairplay and Cass), District 6 (Jefferson 2) and one at-large seat [29, 6]. The district's board page says Shake (Stafford), Decker (Jefferson II) and Brock Hostetter (at large) serve through 2026 [31]. Neither Shake nor Decker is on the ballot [6]. Dyer, appointed to the District 4 seat in January 2026, is running for it [34, 6].

Seat-count and name discrepancy: the Daily World's Sept. 18 ballot list shows the at-large race as one seat, consistent with the state's “vote for 1” [29]. But that list also names incumbent Brock Hostetter (Republican) as an at-large candidate, and the state list does not include him [29, 6]. No fetched source explains the difference, for example a withdrawal.

Party labels: on the state list, Brandon C Deloof, Jan (Johnson) Van Sant, Dustin Stahl and Timothy York are Republican. Scott Cooksey and Brenden Dyer are Independent. Kyla Helms, Tracey (Strickler) Linneweber and Ashley B. (Bingham) Harroll are Nonpartisan [6].

Superintendent turnover: the board voted in February 2025 to hire Jim Larkin as superintendent [35]. He left on Sept. 30, 2025 under a separation agreement, and high school principal Jason Walton was named acting lead administrator [35]. On Oct. 20, 2025 the board voted 7-0 to make Walton interim superintendent [27]. In February 2026 it began drafting a contract for him to serve as full-time superintendent, and it approved that contract 7-0 on March 16, 2026 [36, 28].

Finances and enrollment: in November 2025 the board discussed a one-year teacher contract that allowed no step or column raises for 2025-26 “due to deficit financing”; the board ratified the agreement Nov. 12 [37, 38]. At a Dec. 15, 2025 hearing the business official explained that the board was approving up to $750,000 in additional Education Fund appropriations from cash balances. She said lower-than-projected enrollment had reduced state tuition revenue, and that declining enrollment “remains the primary long-term concern” [39]. In April 2026 the superintendent told the board the effects of SEA 1 (the 2025 property-tax law) were uncertain, with possible cuts to operating funds in coming years [40].

Staffing: the board updated its staff-reduction policy in April 2026 so that seniority is considered first, along with effectiveness, and in June 2026 it acknowledged staffing reductions involving four employees [40, 33]. Parents, staff and residents raised concerns about staff turnover and communication during public comment at the May 18, 2026 meeting [41].

Food service: on July 27, 2026 the board approved hiring Chartwells to run cafeteria operations; the minutes record a 4-1 vote with Roger Weaver abstaining [42]. Administration cited cafeteria staffing problems, and said Chartwells proposed higher wages than the district paid, along with more scratch cooking [42]. A resident who spoke at that meeting questioned the cost and asked about cafeteria electrical safety [42].

Technology and facilities: in May 2026, after a public work session, the board approved a student-device plan (Option Two) that moves from iPads to Neo devices. In April the board had discussed screen time and put the cost at about $350,000–$400,000 [40, 43]. In August 2026 it chose Linton Glass to replace high school door locks and voted to study an early care center at the elementary school, with start-up costs covered by a Greene County Foundation grant [25]. In a September 2026 letter to the Daily World, resident Bruce Porter objected to planned capital spending on field irrigation, tennis courts and middle school HVAC, citing enrollment losses [44].

Homeschool participation: in May 2026 the board voted to let homeschooled students who live in the district take part in athletics, consistent with IHSAA rules, if they enroll in one credit-bearing course [41, 45].

Drama sponsor vote: on May 18, 2026 a recommendation to approve former board member Conner Hill as volunteer drama club sponsor got three yes votes (Dyer, Miranda Hostetter, Weaver), two no votes (Brock Hostetter, Shake) and one abstention (Decker). The board attorney later said the motion failed because four yes votes were needed [41, 33]. Supporters of Hill spoke at the May and June meetings; the board president and superintendent said the matter was settled [46].
Forums: no 2026 WRV candidate forum, questionnaire or candidate statement was found in fetched sources. The Daily World published bios for Bloomfield candidates but none for WRV candidates.

candidates.summary: Incumbent, appointed in January 2026 to the District 4 (Fairplay and Cass) seat vacated by Conner Hill; listed as Independent [6, 47].
background: Is a current board member. The board appointed him on Jan. 19, 2026 to fill the District 4 vacancy left when Conner Hill resigned, after Hill bought a home outside the district he represented. The vote was 4-1, with Roger Weaver opposed [48, 34, 47].
The district's board page says he is serving his first term, appointed to fill a vacancy, and represents the Fairplay and Cass township seat [31].
path_to_ballot: Listed on the state ballot list as Independent for District 4 [6, 29].

items: On May 18, 2026 he moved to let homeschooled students who live in the district take part in athletics, consistent with IHSAA rules, if they enroll in one credit-bearing course; the motion passed unanimously [41].
On May 18, 2026 he moved to approve a partnership with Indiana Wesleyan University to train instructional assistants as licensed teachers; it passed unanimously [41].
On May 18, 2026 he moved to approve Conner Hill as volunteer drama club sponsor and voted yes; the motion failed for lack of four yes votes [41, 33].
On July 27, 2026 he moved to approve Chartwells as the district's food service vendor; the motion passed [42].

In March 2026 he moved to begin negotiations to let the Greene-Sullivan Special Education Cooperative use space at the Lyons facility, and in April he moved to donate an unused modular building to the fire department for training; both passed [28, 40].
